EL PASO, Texas (CNN) -- CNN Hero Maria Ruiz has been changing the lives of children and their families in Juarez, Mexico, for more than 12 years. But lately, it's been Ruiz's own life that's been changing. Crews prepare to demolish Maria Ruiz's home as part of ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition." In November, "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" honored Ruiz for crossing the Texas border to Juarez several times a week to deliver food, clothing and toys to impoverished children and their families. Months later, Ruiz and her family received another surprise, courtesy of ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition." Ruiz, her husband and their two children were sent on a five-day vacation to the Bahamas while thousands of volunteers built the family a custom-designed home. "When Ty Pennington came to our home and said, 'Ruiz family, come on out,' we all just ran out and couldn't believe that we were chosen," Ruiz said. "It's a blessing to us, but we weren't expecting all of this at all, and it has been overwhelming." Pennington is the host of "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition," which selected Ruiz and her family from thousands of applicants throughout Texas. Pennington said the idea was to give Ruiz what she needed most: the tools to do more.  Watch Ruiz and her family react to their new home » . In addition to bringing supplies to the people of Juarez, Ruiz and her family are completing construction of a complex there, which includes a community kitchen, an orphanage and a trade school. Read more about Ruiz's work . In order to devote their time to the Juarez community, the family put construction of their own home on hold in 1996, Ruiz said, leaving many parts unfinished. They were also using much of their living space as a warehouse for all of the donations for the Juarez families, she said. "A home is somewhere you can go after a long day's work and relax and where the family can get together and be able to sit down and talk about our day," Ruiz said. "When we had the things in the living room, we couldn't do that there." Upon returning from the Bahamas, Ruiz and her family were surrounded by thousands of volunteers and community members who blocked them from seeing the changes by the show's large bus. After chanting the show's coined phrase -- "Move that bus!" -- Ruiz and her family were introduced to their new home. "For us, it is a new beginning, and it's going to change our lives," Ruiz said. With her new home, Ruiz will be able to continue -- and even expand -- her family's work for those in need. According to Executive Producer Anthony Dominici, both an additional kitchen and storage space were built in the new home for Ruiz. And "through the generosity of the community," enough donations of food, clothes and toys were collected to fill a 20-foot shipping container and a 16-foot cube truck -- including more than 75,000 cans of food, Dominici said. "That's the whole point here," Pennington said. "To give her what she needs to make her life easier to literally spread dreams and hope to people who have absolutely none of either one of those." For Ruiz, it's about teaching young minds so they can in turn give back to their community. "If you teach them and train them as a child and they go out and do the same, we would live in a much better world." "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" introduced Ruiz to the world when it premiered on Thanksgiving on the global networks of CNN. Actress Selena Gomez introduced and presented Ruiz with her CNN Hero award. Each of the top 10 CNN Heroes also received $25,000.  Watch Ruiz accept her CNN Hero Award » . Nominations for 2009 CNN Heroes opened January 1 and can be submitted at www.CNN.com/Heroes. The Ruiz family episode of "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition" is scheduled to air March 15.

Following the crowd's passionate chant of the show’s iconic catchphrase—"Move that bus!"—the Ruiz family was finally introduced to their transformed sanctuary.

**A House Built on Sacrifice: How Maria Ruiz Transformed Her Home to Feed a Community**

For years, Maria Ruiz lived by a simple, unwavering philosophy: the needs of others must always come before her own. Living on the U.S.–Mexico border, Maria witnessed firsthand the crushing poverty afflicting thousands of families in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. Driven by deep compassion, she made it her life's mission to bring food, clothing, and hope to a community that often felt forgotten by the world.

Maria’s commitment went far beyond occasional volunteering; it became a full-time calling. On a regular basis, she loaded up her vehicle to deliver essential supplies directly to impoverished families across the border. Her dream, however, was not just to provide temporary relief, but to build lasting solutions. Through tireless fundraising and physical labor, Maria managed to construct a full community complex in Juárez, providing local residents with a central gathering place, educational support, and basic services. 

Yet, as she built hope for others, her own living conditions crumbled. For over a decade, Maria and her husband left their personal home completely unfinished. Raw studs, exposed wiring, and bare concrete were the norm, as every spare dollar went toward her ministry in Mexico. Furthermore, her home ceased to function as a family dwelling altogether—nearly every room was converted into a chaotic, makeshift warehouse, packed to the ceilings with donated clothes, canned goods, and household items awaiting transport to Juárez. 

Maria’s extraordinary selflessness did not go unnoticed forever. After her efforts earned her national recognition as a CNN Hero, her inspiring story caught the attention of ABC’s popular television series, *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition*. Recognizing that Maria was a woman who gave everything away while asking for nothing in return, the show’s team—along with a legion of local volunteers—stepped in to perform a life-changing miracle for the Ruiz family.

The team demolished the unfinished structure and replaced it with a stunning, custom-designed home. Crucially, the designers understood that Maria’s passion was her work. In addition to creating a comfortable, fully finished living sanctuary where her family could finally rest, they built specialized facilities into the property specifically tailored to her charitable endeavors. The new build included dedicated, organized storage spaces and a streamlined staging area for donations, replacing the clutter with efficiency.

The transformation provided the Ruiz family with the comfortable, complete home they had deferred for so long, while simultaneously equipping Maria with the professional tools needed to expand her outreach. Today, Maria Ruiz continues her vital work in Juárez, operating from a place of stability and strength—a powerful reminder that true generosity has a way of coming full circle.

Situated at the far western tip of the Lone Star State, this unique area serves as both a focal point for national political debate and a shining example of cross-border community and resilience.

Over the years, CNN coverage of Texas has often captured the complexities of this region. **EL PASO, Texas (CNN) —** For years, Maria Ruiz put everyone else’s needs before her own, turning her modest El Paso home into a bustling, overcrowded staging ground for thousands of pounds of food, clothing, and hope bound for impoverished families across the Mexican border. 

On Thursday, the tables turned for the humble humanitarian in a massive, life-changing way.

As hundreds of local volunteers, builders, and cheering neighbors gathered on her street, the iconic silver coach pulled away to the thunderous chant of "Move that bus!" revealing a brand-new, custom-built home courtesy of ABC’s *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition.*

Ruiz, who was named a top-10 CNN Hero in 2011 for her tireless work feeding and clothing thousands of children in Ciudad Juárez, broke down in tears as she saw the stunning transformation for the first time.

"I have no words, only a heart full of gratitude," Ruiz said, wiping away tears as she gripped the hand of host Ty Pennington. "I always asked God to help me help others. I never imagined He would send an army to help me."

### A home consumed by charity

For more than two decades, Ruiz and her husband, Jesus, lived a life of radical generosity. Multiple times a week, Maria would pack her old pickup truck with donations and drive across the border into some of Juárez's poorest *colonias*, delivering food, toys, and custom-built shoes to families living in extreme poverty.

But her selflessness came at a personal cost. 

Without a dedicated facility for her charity, "Maria's Ministry," her small, aging house had become completely engulfed by her mission. Pallets of pinto beans, sacks of rice, and mountains of donated clothes filled her living room, hallway, and bedrooms. The home was falling apart, plagued by structural issues, inadequate plumbing, and a lack of heating during the desert winter nights. 

There was virtually no space left for the Ruiz family to simply live.

"When we first walked into Maria's home, you couldn't even see the floor—not because of clutter, but because of pure love," Pennington told CNN on set. "She sacrificed her own comfort, her own privacy, and her own living space to feed thousands of kids. We knew we had to give her a home that loved her back."

### Built with love—and a dedicated warehouse

In true *Extreme Makeover* fashion, the weeklong build was a race against the clock. Local builder Casa Ford partnered with hundreds of community volunteers who worked around the clock, battling blazing Texas temperatures to demolish the old, unsafe structure and erect a modern, state-of-the-art residence in just seven days.

The new property was specifically tailored to solve the family's unique challenge: separating their personal life from their massive outreach efforts.

The front of the property now features a beautiful, Spanish-colonial-style family home, complete with an open-concept kitchen, energy-efficient solar panels, and comfortable bedrooms where Maria and Jesus can finally rest.

Crucially, the back of the property now houses a custom-designed, 2,000-square-foot staging warehouse. Equipped with industrial shelving, walk-in refrigeration units, and a covered loading dock, the new facility will allow Maria to expand her ministry and streamline her relief trips to Juárez without sacrificing her home.

"This isn't just a house for Maria and her family; it's a launchpad for hope," said one of the project's lead designers. "Now she can store ten times the food, keep perishable goods fresh, and load her truck safely."

### Two worlds, one mission

The collaboration marks a rare, heartwarming crossover moment between network television entertainment and global humanitarian recognition, uniting the spirit of CNN Heroes with the transformational power of *Extreme Makeover*.

For the people of El Paso and Juárez, the new home is a fitting tribute to a woman who has become a symbol of cross-border compassion.

As Ruiz walked through the doors of her new home, holding her grandchildren close, she made it clear that her work is far from over. If anything, she said, this new beginning is just fuel for the road ahead.

"The doors of this house will always be open," Ruiz said, looking out at the crowd of volunteers who made it possible. "We have a lot of work to do, and now, we can do so much more."

Here is the story of Maria Ruiz, her mission, and the incredible makeover that changed her life.

---

### The Mission: A Heart Without Borders

For decades, Ciudad Juárez—just across the Rio Grande from El Paso—was plagued by extreme poverty, worsened by the violence of drug cartel wars. While many people avoided the border city, Maria Ruiz saw a desperate need that she couldn't ignore. 

In the late 1990s, Maria began crossing the border into some of Juárez's poorest *colonias* (slums). She saw children eating out of trash cans and families living in shacks made of cardboard and pallets, lacking clean water, electricity, and basic food. 

Driven by her faith and deep empathy, Maria and her husband, Jesus, made it their life’s mission to help. Every week for over 15 years, Maria would:
* Feed hundreds of impoverished children.
* Hand out clothing, shoes, blankets, and toys.
* Deliver basic medical supplies and food staples like rice and beans.

Even during the darkest years of Juárez’s drug war, when the city was considered one of the most dangerous in the world, Maria never stopped crossing the border. She famously said that love was stronger than fear.

### The Sacrifice at Home

While Maria was nourishing thousands of people in Mexico, her own family was making massive sacrifices. 

Their modest El Paso home was completely overrun by her mission. Every room—including the bedrooms, living room, and hallway—was crammed to the ceiling with boxes of donated clothes, non-perishable food, and supplies. Maria and her family barely had room to sleep or sit. 

To make matters worse, their home was falling apart. It had severe structural problems, poor heating, and a failing roof. Maria poured every extra penny she and her husband earned into buying food for the children of Juárez, leaving nothing left to fix her own house. 

### The *Extreme Makeover* Surprise

In 2009, community members who were moved by Maria's relentless selflessness nominated the Ruiz family for *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition*. 

In early 2010, Ty Pennington and his crew arrived in El Paso with his famous bullhorn to yell, *"Good morning, Ruiz family!"* 

The show recognized that Maria didn't just need a house; she needed a functional space to continue her humanitarian work. During the one-week build, hundreds of local volunteers and builders came together to transform the Ruiz property.

### The New Home and "The Warehouse of Hope"

When the bus moved, revealing the new home, Maria was brought to tears. The team had built:
1. **A Beautiful Family Home:** A modern, safe, and spacious multi-bedroom home for Maria, Jesus, and their family, giving them a restful, peaceful place to live for the first time in decades.
2. **A Dedicated Community Warehouse:** On the same property, the team built a separate, massive storage facility and staging area. This allowed Maria to organize donations, pack her truck, and run her charity efficiently—without turning her personal living space into a warehouse.
3. **Surprise Donations:** The show and its sponsors surprised Maria with a brand-new, heavy-duty truck to transport goods across the border, as well as thousands of dollars worth of food, supplies, and educational materials for the children of Juárez.

### Her Legacy

The exposure from *Extreme Makeover* brought worldwide attention to Maria’s organization, **Maria Ruiz Ministries** (often working alongside Heart of the World). Donations poured in from across the United States, allowing her to expand her reach to build daycares, feeding centers, and schools in Juárez.

Maria Ruiz’s story remains one of the most memorable in the history of *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition*—a powerful reminder of how one ordinary person’s extraordinary love can transform thousands of lives across international borders.

For more than a decade, Ruiz, 55, has quietly organized and driven weekly relief missions across the International Bridge into Ciudad Juárez, Mexico—a city plagued in recent years by severe economic hardship and escalating drug cartel violence. Undeterred by border danger or financial strain, Ruiz packs her pickup truck and personal van with food, clothing, toys, and basic necessities, delivering them directly to impoverished families living in dusty *colonias* on the outskirts of Juárez.

Ruiz’s tireless efforts reached millions of viewers Thursday night during the broadcast of *"CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute,"* hosted by Anderson Cooper. 

Teen sensation and Texas native Selena Gomez took the stage to introduce Ruiz, presenting a heartfelt tribute to the woman known affectionately in the borderlands as an "angel of mercy."

"Maria doesn't look at the border as a barrier; she looks at it as a bridge," Gomez told the audience. "In a place where so many people feel forgotten, she brings food, warmth, and most importantly, hope. To see someone from my home state dedicate her entire life so selflessly to children and families in Juárez is truly inspiring to my generation."

Ruiz’s journey began humbly when she noticed children scouring garbage dumps in Juárez for food. Alongside her husband and children, she began converting her own home into a collection center, spending her weekends baking hundreds of loaves of bread and collecting donated goods from her El Paso community. Over the years, her grass-roots outreach, "Feed the Children in the Colonias," has provided tens of thousands of hot meals, clothing, and holiday toys to children who otherwise would go without.

The emotional tribute drew praise from Hollywood figures and TV veterans attending the event, including *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition* host Ty Pennington, who commended Ruiz’s hands-on work ethic and determination.

"What Maria does every single week is just mind-blowing," Pennington said backstage during the event. "She isn't sitting back waiting for someone else to step up or waiting on a massive budget. She gets in her truck, rolls up her sleeves, and drives right into the heart of where people need help the most. That kind of relentless, boots-on-the-ground energy is what real building and rebuilding of lives is all about."

Television producer Anthony Dominici, who worked on the broadcast, emphasized the powerful narrative Ruiz brought to this year's lineup of extraordinary everyday citizens.

"When you look at Maria’s story, you're reminded of the sheer power of one individual's determination," Dominici noted. "Capturing her journey and bringing her quiet heroism from the dusty streets of Juárez to a global stage was profoundly moving for our entire production team. She embodies the absolute best of what human beings can do for one another when driven purely by love."

Despite the Hollywood spotlights, red carpet glamor, and a $25,000 grant awarded to each top hero, Ruiz remained unfailingly modest. Through tears, she dedicated the honor to the children of Juárez and stressed that her mission is far from complete.

"This recognition isn't for me; it's for the children who wake up hungry every day," Ruiz said following the ceremony. "As long as God gives me the strength and a working truck, I will keep crossing that bridge."

The story of **Maria Ruiz**, often referred to as the **"Angel of Juárez,"** gained widespread national attention in 2011 through coverage by **CNN** (as part of their *CNN Heroes* initiative) and a special episode of ABC's ***Extreme Makeover: Home Edition***. 

Here is a summary of the story, her work, and how CNN and *Extreme Makeover* were involved:

---

### **Who is Maria Ruiz?**
Maria Ruiz is a law firm employee from El Paso, Texas. For over two decades, she devoted her life to helping impoverished children and families across the border in **Ciudad Juárez, Mexico**—a city that, at the time, was considered one of the most violent cities in the world due to brutal drug cartel wars.

Despite the severe danger, Maria and her family regularly drove across the U.S.–Mexico border into some of Juárez's poorest neighborhoods to distribute:
* Food, clothing, and shoes
* School supplies and toys
* Medical supplies
* Financial support for local families

She also helped build a daycare center and a school in Juárez so children would have a safe place to go while their parents worked in local factories (*maquiladoras*).

---

### **The CNN Connection (*CNN Heroes*)**
In 2011, CNN named Maria Ruiz one of its **Top 10 CNN Heroes** of the year. 

CNN’s articles and video reports highlighted her extreme bravery and selflessness. While fear of cartel violence kept many aid organizations away from Juárez, Maria continued her weekly trips. CNN reported that her efforts were feeding and supporting over 2,000 children every month.

The national exposure from CNN brought her story to a massive audience, inspiring people across the United States to donate to her mission.

---

### **The *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition* Episode**
Following her recognition, the popular TV show ***Extreme Makeover: Home Edition* (Season 9, Episode 10)** stepped in to help her family and expand her charity work.

* **The Problem:** Maria’s modest home in El Paso was completely overwhelmed. Her yard, garage, and living space were packed to the ceiling with donated food, clothes, and supplies, leaving almost no living space for her husband, children, and grandchildren.
* **The Makeover:** Host Ty Pennington and the *Extreme Makeover* team, along with thousands of local El Paso volunteers, built the Ruiz family a brand-new home. 
* **The Facility:** Crucially, the team also constructed a **dedicated warehouse and community distribution center** on the property. This allowed Maria to store, organize, and pack donations safely and efficiently without cluttering her personal home.

### **Key Takeaways from the Coverage**
* **Courage in a War Zone:** Both CNN and *Extreme Makeover* emphasized that Maria was doing humanitarian work in an area that many government officials and NGOs deemed too dangerous to enter.
* **Family Effort:** The media coverage highlighted that her efforts were a family affair, supported heavily by her husband, Jesus, and her children.
* **Lasting Impact:** The new facilities provided by *Extreme Makeover* and the funding generated by CNN’s platform enabled her organization (*Hands Across the Barricade*) to scale up operations and help even more families in Juárez.

**BUILT ON KINDNESS: HOW A TV MAKEOVER TURNED ONE HUMANITARIAN’S HOME INTO A COMMUNITY LIFELINE**

**By Elena Rostova**  
*Community Feature Correspondent*

**OAKDALE —** Six months ago, walking from the front door to the kitchen in Maya Lin’s modest three-bedroom bungalow required a delicate, zigzagging dance. 

Canned goods were stacked like Jenga towers along the hallway. Winter coats, destined for local shelters, spilled off the dining room table. Boxes of diapers sat stacked to the ceiling in her spare bedroom, leaving barely enough space for Lin to unwind after a 12-hour day of community outreach.

"My home was no longer a home," says Lin, 42, founder of *Hope Delivered*, a grassroots mutual-aid initiative. "It was a cramped, chaotic warehouse. But every time I thought about stopping, I’d picture the families depending on us. I just couldn’t say no to a donation."

Today, Lin’s house is still full of supplies—but the chaos is gone. Thanks to a surprise visit from the hit home renovation show *Blueprint for Good*, Lin’s house has been transformed into a state-of-the-art community hub, expanding her reach and proving that functional design can double as an act of service.

---

### **A Breaking Point**

Lin’s journey began four years ago during a harsh winter when she started delivering care packages out of her trunk to unhoused neighbors. What started as a personal passion project quickly snowballed into a massive operation. Last year alone, *Hope Delivered* distributed over 15,000 pounds of food and essential goods across the metro area.

However, without the funds to rent a commercial warehouse, Lin turned her residence into the initiative’s base of operations. 

"I was storing sacks of rice under my bed," Lin admits with a self-deprecating laugh. "I was turning down bulk donations—like a pallet of fresh produce from a local farm—simply because I had nowhere to keep them cold, and nowhere to put them."

Unknown to Lin, her volunteers and neighbors were watching her burn out. Secretly, they nominated her for *Blueprint for Good*, a reality television show that redevelops homes for local heroes.

---

### **The Transformation**

When host Marcus Vance and his design crew knocked on Lin’s door last September, they didn’t just bring paint swatches and throw pillows—they brought structural engineers and commercial storage specialists.

Over the course of a whirlwind ten-day renovation, the crew completely re-imagined the layout of Lin’s property. 

The biggest change took place in the detached, underutilized garage and back patio. The team insulated, climate-controlled, and wired the space, turning it into a mini-distribution center. Equipped with industrial-grade stainless steel shelving, commercial walk-in refrigeration units, and smooth, polished concrete floors for rolling carts, the new "Hope Hub" instantly professionalized Lin’s operation.

Inside the main house, the designers drew a firm line between Lin’s public mission and her private life. They installed custom, hidden floor-to-ceiling cabinetry in the entryways to discreetly hold overflow items, while completely restoring her living room and master bedroom into tranquil, donation-free sanctuaries.

"Humanitarian workers suffer from immense burnout," said Vance during the episode's reveal. "Maya spends all day taking care of others. We wanted to give her a space that takes care of her, while giving her organization room to bloom."

---

### **Multiplying the Impact**

When Lin saw the final result, she broke down in tears. "They didn't just give me my home back," she says. "They gave this community a future."

The structural changes yielded immediate real-world results. With the addition of commercial refrigeration, *Hope Delivered* can now accept fresh dairy, meat, and produce from local supermarkets that previously would have gone to waste. The streamlined sorting layout has allowed volunteer efficiency to skyrocket.

According to Lin, the impact was felt almost instantly:

* **Capacity Tripled:** The initiative now holds three times the volume of non-perishable goods.
* **Expanded Outreach:** The group has scaled up from serving 80 families a week to more than 250.
* **New Programs:** With proper storage, Lin launched a "Dignity Kit" initiative, providing hygiene and baby products that were previously too bulky to stock.

On a recent Tuesday afternoon, half a dozen volunteers were busy in the renovated garage, effortlessly packing boxes along an ergonomic assembly line. Laughter echoed off the walls—a stark contrast to the cramped stress of months past.

"It’s completely changed our momentum," says Sarah Jenkins, a long-time volunteer. "Before, we spent half our time moving boxes just to find other boxes. Now, we walk in, get to work, and get help to the people who need it in half the time."

---

### **A Model for the Future**

For Lin, the makeover was never about getting a fancy kitchen or TV-ready interiors. It was about validation—a sign that the work she and her team are doing matters. 

As she sits in her newly restored living room, sipping tea in a room entirely free of cardboard boxes, Lin reflects on the journey.

"The show gave us the hardware," Lin says, looking out the window toward the busy, bright green garage. "But the community provides the heart. Now that we have the space to match our ambition, there's no limit to how many people we can reach."
